title: War, Witness and Two Centuries Apart
welcome_lead: Compare two poems of war and witness — Wilfred Owen and Carol Ann Duffy — to see how poetic ethics evolves across the long century.
meta_desc: A-Level Comparative Poetry adventure on war and witness: Wilfred Owen and Carol Ann Duffy.
final_note: Owen wrote from the trench; Duffy writes from the news cycle. Both refuse the consolation of heroism.

walkthroughs.body_html: Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est' (composed 1917, published 1920 posthumously) recounts a gas attack and dies on a Latin tag: Horace's 'it is sweet and right to die for one's country' is exposed as 'the old Lie'. Duffy's 'War Photographer' depicts a returning photojournalist developing prints in a darkroom; the poem closes on his editor selecting 'five or six' for the Sunday supplement. Both poems indict comfortable distance: the schoolboy reader in Owen, the breakfast reader in Duffy.

'Dulce et Decorum Est' uses 28 lines in irregular quatrains and longer stanzas, with broken iambic pentameter that physically performs exhaustion. 'War Photographer' uses four six-line stanzas of disciplined rhyme (ABBCDD), the formal control ironising the disorder it represents. Comparison: Owen's metre fractures under content; Duffy's metre holds, exposing the editor's professional containment. Both poems use form to dramatise their ethical claims.

Owen speaks as participant — 'I' is the soldier-witness. Duffy speaks as observer of an observer — third-person external. Both stage the problem of representation. Critics including Geoff Dyer (The Missing of the Somme, 1994) and Susan Sontag (Regarding the Pain of Others, 2003) frame the question: what does it mean to make art from others' suffering? Comparative analysis can use Sontag to put Owen and Duffy into theoretical contact.
